7.15.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
When Huṇḍa and Tuhuṇḍa were slain by Vināyaka,
that battle between the lords of the gaṇas and the asuras became tumultuous. / 1
Roaring like clouds filled with water at the coming of the rains,
they quickly destroyed one another as they fought. / 2
Their limbs drenched in flowing streams of blood, their lips bitten by teeth,
they struck one another with tridents, spears, rṣṭis, and paṭṭiśas. / 3
Hearing the ear-rending sounds of spears being thrown, swords falling,
names being proclaimed, and bows twanging, / 4
Jambha, foremost among the mighty, enraged by the slaughter of his brothers,
entered the Pramatha host. / 5

7.15.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Withdrawing then from the battle, Andhaka, the foremost of the asuras,
approached Śukra and, with bowed head, spoke these words: / 1
‘O lord, having taken refuge in you, we count the gods together with their followers
as equal to blades of grass; I speak the truth always. / 2
As elephants [fear] lions, or serpents [fear] Garuḍas,
the gods are always afraid of us through your grace. / 3
Protected by you, the daityas entered without fear
the gods' impenetrable battle array, like those afflicted by heat [entering] a lake. / 4
Taking refuge in you, standing firm like unshakeable stones,
we strike Indra in battle without hesitation, O best of brahmins. / 5
And in times of distress, together with our wives and sons,
we serve day and night your feet that bestow happiness. / 6
Do you ever protect us who have come to you for refuge
in times of danger, like another Nārāyaṇa [protects] the gods! / 7
Look at Huṇḍa, Tuhuṇḍa, Kujambha, and Jambha,
Pāka, Kārtasvana, and the great asura Vipāka! / 8

7.15.m: Huṇḍa, Tuhuṇḍa, Jambha, and the great Asura Kujambha, / those enemies of the gods, fought with blows of rocks, spears, and stones. / And those two, Pāka and Indradamana, and the mighty Kārtasvana, / crushed the Pramatha host out of a desire to exact vengeance. / Having checked their speed, the Pramathas too, haughty, / holding rocks and trees in their hands, all rushed against the Dānavas. / But of the Gaṇa lords and the gods in that exceedingly terrifying battle, / the sounds of bows and the frightful sounds of chariots were heard. / Some intent on the victory of the Pramathas, and likewise others [intent on that] of the Dānavas, / made a dreadful tumult and partisan shouts in the sky. / The sound of the armies roaring and charging was / like that of oceans roaring and rushing at the dissolution. / And Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Cāraṇas, intoxicated by the excellence of the battle, / shouted and cast down various heaps of flowers. / Various kinds of flowers falling shone forth / when released by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas, like stars at the dissolution. / The musical instruments of the gods and Gandharvas sounded repeatedly, / and ceased again and again as their minds were riveted upon the battle. / But Jambha, remembering in the battle his defeat by Vināyaka, / charged angrily at him, like an elephant against another elephant.

7.15.m:
Seeing that Dānava Jambha charging in battle, / Vināyaka blocked him, as an angry lion blocks an elephant. / Raising his trunk, which resembled the trunk of Airāvata, / Vināyaka, who has an elephant-like face, struck the Dānava in battle.
Then Jambha, that elephant among Dānavas, with an excellent arrow, / pierced him between his two frontal globes, just as a Siddha [pierces] the solar disc.
That arrow sank deep between his two frontal lobes, / like a lightning-bearing cloud between the twin peaks of the king of mountains. / With his mind enraged by the arrow, shaking his trunk and head, / bending down and striking the great Daitya with the tip of his trunk, he roared.

Trembling from being struck by Vināyaka's trunk, / Jambha, enraged, covered Vināyaka with fierce arrows. / Like locusts entering a field, or bees entering a tree, / Jambha's arrows then entered the god Vināyaka.
Dripping blood, with their points cleaving [his body], / the arrows shone on Vināyaka like serpents clinging to Mount Meru.
With his limbs severely pierced by Jambha's arrows, his red eyes bathed in the blood streaming from his frontal lobes, / the god shook his trunk-tip and head, and rushed at Jambha as a thirsty man rushes to water. / Repeatedly striking him hard with his strong trunk-tip and repeatedly roaring, / the mighty one then seized the chariot in the battle and hurled it away along with its horses, banner, weapons, and wheels.

7.15.m: Agitating the Daityas, that bull-king Nandin seized Śukra, who was being protected by those sons of Diti armed with nooses, swords, trees, stones, and spears, just as a śarabha seizes an elephant. / His garment slipping down, his ornaments fallen off, his hair disheveled, held fast by the enemy, the enemies of the gods rushed forward roaring like lions as if about to release him. / Those lords of the Dānavas poured down upon Nandīśvara a shower of thunderbolts, tridents, arrows, battle-axes, and trembling weapons accompanied by discs, staves, and rocks, like fierce rain-clouds. / Having reached the descendant of Bhṛgu, that foremost leader of the gaṇas, having incinerated hundreds of weapons with the fire of his mouth, Nandīśvara departed, holding in his hand Śukra, the protector of the host of Dānavas. / Then between them there ensued a great battle, causing deep satisfaction to the minds of the gods, with fearful falls of discharged missiles and weapons, as they shouted, 'Slay!' and 'Seize!' / Meanwhile, having approached Bhava's side, Nandīśvara, his eyes discolored with rage, quickly announced to Bhava, 'Lord, here is that Śukra!' / And that god of gods accepted Śukra as an offering given by a pure person; without saying anything, the guardian of beings swallowed Śukra, his enemy, who stood in his mouth. / Then his leaders of gaṇas once again smote the army of the Dānavas and Daityas. / Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, on the abduction of the descendant of Bhṛgu during the battle of the gaṇas, in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.15.m: "By Nandin courageously carrying off Śukra, the best of leaders, the lives of us all have surely been stolen away today. / Who will revive again the Daityas slain by the Pramathas? Without that descendant of Bhṛgu, Śukra, who else will sustain us? / Resolution, valor, splendor, vitality, vigor, strength, and constancy—everything has been stolen by the enemies when the divine Śukra was carried away. / Since the divine descendant of Bhṛgu has been abducted, my mind too is afflicted; yet I shall not abandon the conflict when assailed by the Pramathas. / Steady yourselves, do not fear, fight with the enemies! I shall destroy all the Pramathas along with Nandin! / Today, having rendered them helpless and having slain the thirty gods as well, I shall liberate the descendant of Bhṛgu like a lion trapped in a cage. / And he, an ascetic, if the master himself should emerge from his body by means of yoga, shall be protected by the rest of us!" / Hearing these words of Andhaka, the Dānavas, roaring like clouds, tormented the Pramathas, having made their resolve to die.

Kujambha cut his sword in two, as Garuḍa [cuts] a serpent; / and then with a blood-stained arm, with a well-drawn arrow, / Kujambha struck him on the arm, like Indra [striking] a mountain with his thunderbolt. / Hard hit by him, he staggered like a sāla tree.

Vyāsa said: / Once that brahmin, Bhārgava, was swallowed by the bearer of the crescent moon, / what did he do while staying within the belly of that god of gods? / And how did that twice-born, best among the austere, a yogin endowed with great tapas, / not emerge from the god's body by the power of yoga? / And how did Andhaka, the foremost of the Asuras, surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas, / offer battle at that time without Bhārgava?
Tell me all this in full, O best among the knowers of the entire Veda; / there is no satiety for me as I listen to the deeds of the Lord. / Sūta said: / When Vyāsa asked in this manner, Sanatkumāra, best among sages, / recounted the deeds of Śukra. / Sanatkumāra said: / When Bhārgava was swallowed by that friend of Umā and the gods, / Andhaka lost his luster, like the sun blocked by a cloud.

Seeing his army repeatedly broken by the pramathas, / Andhaka himself mounted his chariot and rushed at the gaṇas. / Under those blows of thunderbolt-like arrows, like mountains struck by thunderbolts, / the pramathas fell on the earth like clouds drained of water. / In their chests, thighs, cheeks, / backs, arms, and bellies, / pierced by arrows, the pramathas wailed like elephants. / Going, coming, not yet arrived, arrived, or standing far off— / whatever he saw, wherever he saw it, he pierced it deeply with arrows.
He pierced a hundred with one [arrow], and again a hundred with a hundred, / a thousand with a thousand, and likewise a crore with a crore.

Banners, standards, parasols, / victory flags, goads, housing-cloths, / fly-whisks, diadems, / earrings, and garments—
whatever in the pramathas' army trembled or ran, / the Dānava Andhaka swiftly cut all that down with arrows.
Just as fire [releases] sparks, as a cloud [releases] torrents of rain, / as the ocean [releases] surges, as the sun [releases] rays,
as lions [release] roars in the forest, as elephants [release] spray, / he discharged sharp-pointed arrows that crushed the enemy army.
When Andhaka, the foremost Asura, fought with resolve, / the Asuras too fought with resolve following Andhaka. / Those Nivātakavacas, who closely resembled one another, / in great numbers engaged in battle together with many Rudras.
Sixty thousand Kāleyas, great Asuras resembling Death, / fought together with sixty thousand pramathas born from [his] arms.

7.15.m: Vyāsa said: / The illusory power and the strength of Andhaka, enemy of the gods, / had been created fully by the Blessed One, caused by [his] divine form. / When the sage Bhārgava was swallowed into his body by the god, / what did he do there inside the body of the God of gods? / And how did that twice-born son of Bhṛgu emerge, / by the power of austerity and the power of yoga, like the moon from a white cloud? / This curiosity has arisen in me today, O best of sages: / recount the deeds of Īśāna and of the wise Bhārgava. / Sūta said: / Thus addressed by Vyāsa, the lord Sanatkumāra, son of the lotus-born [Brahmā], / related the emergence of Śukra from Śiva. / Inside the body of Śambhu at that time, Śukra, stripped of his luster, / wandering about seeking an opening, was homeless like the wind.

Wandering inside the belly of Bhava for a hundred years, / he found no opening, just as the Kali age finds no flaw in a pure man. / The Great God also stripped away his yoga / along with its sovereign power and qualities such as animan, though his mind and speech were restrained. / Then a great sound arose from the armies of the pramathas and the asuras; / hearing that sound, the Bhārgava became alarmed and was aroused. / Being inside the husband of Umā, that brahmin, strengthened by austerity, / praised the god Soma, adorned with the crescent moon, with beloved hymns of praise. / To him who had fallen into distress, the trident-bearing god / bestowed the dawn of his favor, saying: 'Go forth through my liṅga!'
Then assuming a subtle form, that Śukra, best among sages, / issued forth like semen (śukra) from the liṅga of the wise God of gods.

And when the Daityas entered the ocean, the abode of sea monsters, / the descendant of Bhṛgu, endowed with immense radiance, flared up like a fire.
Enraged, he cursed the Daityas who had made the ocean their abode: / “Because, abandoning your allies and me, who wished your welfare like a father,
you, powerless, have entered the reservoir of waters to save your lives, / therefore, right there, shameless ones, struck by my curse,
you shall attain the state of fish, born again and again. / As long as worlds, mountains, and oceans exist,
so long shall you become fish, creatures of the water, dwelling in the sea. / Eating human flesh, sinful ones, you shall be eaten by humans.
You shall spend a hundred crore years under my curse!” / Having thus cursed the rest into dwelling in the waters of the ocean,
Śukra of great splendour, brilliant as the moon, fell silent.
Sanatkumāra said: / Then those Asuras, struck by the curse of their guru, were seen
in the waters of the ocean, armed, armoured, and mail-clad.

Then, as the Asuras entered the ocean and were slain by the followers of Śaṅkara, / Andhaka held back all the Pramathas, as an ocean of abundant waters checks rivers.
Then Andhaka pierced Nandin with twelve [arrows], and the fire-born [Skanda] with five; / the Dānava struck Viśākha and Śākha with ten, and Naigameṣa with a hundred.
He pierced Vīrabhadra and Viṭpati, and the radiant Piṅgala, best of Yakṣas, / with arrows adorned with gold, just as an elephant driver goads an elephant with the points of an ankuśa.
There was no one, whether in front or behind, neither horse nor elephant nor any other Pramatha, / who did not receive the arrows shot by Andhaka, resembling blazing cosmic fire and the sun.
Pierced repeatedly like sandalwood trees on their arms, bellies, chests, and heads, / the delighters of their foes stood motionless, like elephants trapped in a cage.
Then lion-roars were raised by the Asuras, fierce with the sounds of conches, hundreds of kettle-drums, and dundubhis; / and again a terrifying battle broke out between the lords of the Gaṇas and the lords of the Dānavas.
Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the battle of the Gaṇas, on the curse of the Asuras.

Attacked by the descending gods, that army of the Dānavas was churned, / like a lake filled with fish whose waters have diminished is churned by royal swans.
Then an exceedingly terrifying clamor arose / in the agitated army of the Dānavas occupied by the gods.
As the water of the ocean [is disturbed] by whales, as the sky by clouds, / as the body by phlegm and bile, as serpents by garuḍas,
so that host of Andhaka was made by the power of the dwellers of heaven / in an instant to have its armor and banners shattered and rendered helpless.
On one side by the gods accompanied by Indra, and on the other by the lords of the Gaṇas, / the Dānava army was struck down, like a flock of goats by hundreds of wolves.

The god with the thunderbolt raised in his hand, the bull among the gods, / went before them, like the syllable Om before the Vedas.
With the fire of his thunderbolt weapon Indra burned the enemies in battle, / just as the fire of expiation burns all sins.
When his army was being slain by the gods and by the Pramathas, / Andhaka, the lord of the Dānavas, blinded by anger and passion, spoke to the Dānavas:
"Having engendered enmity with Rudra, the protector of all the worlds, / it is not possible for those who are dispirited to conquer the Pramathas along with the immortals.
And you must not fear death! Fight, Daityas and Dānavas! / For here stands Bhārgava, who will bring us back to life!
Therefore, having no pity for your lives, / ward off without hesitation the lords of the Gaṇas of the gods according to your strength and enthusiasm!
With many secret illusions, you who possess secret forms, / hold back in battle all these assembled gods!"
Having been thus addressed, […] / […] made terrible [sounds] like clouds at the end of an aeon.

Then, recovering after a long time, the highly renowned husband of Suyaśā, / lifting a powerful thunderbolt, hurled it at Andhaka.
That mighty thunderbolt arriving like fire and the sun, / Andhaka stopped with floods of arrows and laughed aloud.
As he laughed, from his fine-browed eyes drops of tears / flowed down, like rays from the sun's blazing orb.
Then the king of spirits, uprooting a tree with agitated foliage, / said, 'You are slain, O Andhaka!' and hurled it and roared.

When the tree was destroyed, Nandī then tore up the peak of Mandara / filled with deer, wild beasts, and serpents, and ran toward Andhaka in battle.
Nandī, whose home is in the forests on mountain peaks, / brought down that mountain peak onto his chariot, like the slayer of Ahi hurling a thunderbolt onto the Vindhya.
Struck forcefully by Nandī with that peak, / that chariot, along with its wheels, yoke-pole, and horses, turned to dust.
Then, seeing Andhaka's chariot crushed along with its wheels and axles, / the gods with the Gandharvas and the Pramathas with the Guhyakas roared.
Then Andhaka, roaring like a storm-cloud of dissolution, struck Nandī / with a trident, as a lord of elephants strikes a tree.
Struck with the trident, the favorite of the Trident-bearer, / Nandī, his limbs trembling in distress, shook like the moon reflected in water.
As Nandīśvara was reeling, severely afflicted by the blow, / a chorus of lion-roars arose repeatedly in the army of the Asuras.
Roused by that lion-roar of the enemies, / Nandī, the kinsman of the spirits, struck Andhaka with an axe.
Struck by the axe, the Dānava Andhaka shed blood, / as a sandalwood tree struck by an elephant's tusk sheds red sap.

Seeing Andhaka deprived of his chariot, the foes of the gods protected him, / just as the gods, stationed in the directions, protect this world. / Then Bāṇa, son of Bali, brilliant as the bāṇa flower, / that Dānava provided Andhaka with chariot transport. / Then Andhaka, lord of the Dānavas, mounted that chariot, / as the blessed sun, with full disc, mounts the mountain of dawn.
Then battle was joined again by the gods and Dānavas wishing to wage dreadful combat; / fanned by tridents, vajras, thunderbolts, and arrows in the fray, the blazing fire shone exceedingly.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the duel between Andhaka and Nandī.

7.15.m: Others took refuge with Śākha and Viśākha, and others with Kumāra; / taking refuge, the gods stood like birds upon trees. / Just as mortals [tremble] in fear of thunderbolts, as deer in fear of a lion, / and as serpents ever [tremble] before the serpent-devouring Garuḍa, / so the gods, standing in battle, trembled before Andhaka, the enemy of deities; / afflicted by the shower of arrows, they wandered as if bewildered. / Just as a forest of bandhujīva shines, laden with blossoms, / so that attendant army shone, its limbs bathed in blood from wounds. / Just as trees tremble in forests, stirred by the wind, / so the gods were terrified on the battlefield from fear of Andhaka. / Then the mighty Nārāyaṇa, Ananta, and Indra, / the two Aśvins, the eight Vasus, and the twelve Ādityas, / Nandin, Viśākha, Śākha, Vīrabhadra, Prabhāmaya, / Viṭpati, Śaṅkukarṇa, Somanandin, and Vināyaka— / as their army was being struck down by Andhaka with waves of force, / these gods, taking up their weapons, ran toward that lord of the dānava host. / Surrounding his excellent chariot, which resembled a city of the Gandharvas, / they smashed it and roared like rain-clouds.

7.15.m: and Nandin with his fist, Prabhāmaya with a paṭṭiśa, / Pūṣan with a broad-headed arrow, and Yama with a mace. / Having swiftly struck all his enemies in battle, Andhaka / leaped up into the sky and bellowed like a cloud drunk with water. / That deceptive fighter, who resembled a mountain, released mountain-peaks, / filled with trees, bushes, and serpents, and roared aloud. / That terrible rain of mountain-summits, along with trees, bears, and great serpents, / fell upon the armies of the gods, like cold frost upon lotuses. / Without pause, without rest, without breath, bewildered by terror, / […] / with noses, eyes, teeth, and lips severed, legs, hips, and arms broken, / terrified, bewildered, and trembling, the Pramathas and immortals were seen. / Raining palace-peaks, stones, and weapons, repeatedly casting them down, the Asura shone in the sky; / […] / […] sound, / a great lotus covered in smoke, and great fiery dust like fireflies. / With a roar like an overflowing, swollen ocean, situated in the sky, that enemy of the hosts of deities / repeatedly poured down a great torrent of water, just as a rain-cloud pours a fierce shower at the end of time. / Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in [the section of] the battle with Andhaka. / Sanatkumāra said: / Then Andhaka, standing in the sky like a mass of great clouds, / ceased that rain of stones just as a cloud [stops] its rain.

7.15.m:
Seizing once more a bow resembling the great bow of Indra, / he unleashed a storm of arrows, and a deep tempest arose. / Then, [arrows] winged with eagle feathers, adorned with eagle plumes, / flying like eagles, with points sharp as an eagle's beak, / a hundred body-piercing arrows, feeding on the marrow of bodies, / the lord of Dānavas discharged, and he roared in pride.
Sped from the fully drawn bow, encompassing [the sky] as they moved in battle, / guiding their own paths, in speed equal to the mind and wind, / those great arrows of Andhaka fell upon the deities, / just as rays cast by the sun fall upon great mountains. / Elephants were struck by the arrows, horses were struck by the arrows, / and deities and leaders of the Gaṇas were struck on all sides. / With entrails and blood protruding, their garlands and ornaments scattered, / their hair-bindings loosed, they fell in deep agony.
Standing, moving, risen, running, or leaping— / whatever horse, elephant, or god he saw anywhere, / Andhaka forcibly struck down that enemy / with arrows that were the very form of the sun's foe, and bellowed like a cloud at the coming of the rains.
Filled with the cries of the wounded, its horses wandering astray, / with the sound of musical instruments silenced, the army appeared like a river.

7.15.m:
Scattered, severed, torn, burnt, devoured, and tossed about, / [it was] like a forest whose trees were destroyed by an elephant blinded by rut. / Some were struck in the face, and others in the eyes; / others were struck in the chest and belly, and likewise in the back.
Just as spiked clubs are set closely together, so the hosts of the Maruts were pierced with arrows; / and the gaṇas of terrible valor, when struck, did not reach the ground.
Then a river carrying the water of wounds was set in motion by the gods and asuras, / crowded with alligator-like lordly elephants, with chariot-wheels for beautiful tortoises, / with severed elephant-trunks for serpents, bows and banner-poles for excellent trees, / crests of diadems for frogs, and bowstrings for its moss.

With scattered pearl necklaces for gravel, and white garments for immense foam, / set in motion by the gods and asuras, it was exceedingly hard for gods and asuras to cross.
Then piśācas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas, having the luster of collyrium and grinning with lightning-like smiles, / intensely tormented by thirst, / drank that blood just as gods drink excellent nectar. / Then once more there arose a tumultuous and wondrous battle, / as Nandī was pierced by Andhaka with a great arrow.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, in the description of the battlefield.
